VIDEO.title: Why Paul Preached the Gospel to Christians AGAIN | Romans 1
VIDEO.series: The Book of Romans, Every Word (playlist of 28 videos)

kicker: Study aid · Romans 1:1-15 · Episode 1 (#1 of 28 in the playlist)
hand: A slave of Christ, in debt to grace
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Romans 1:1-15. Paul introduces himself as a slave of Christ Jesus, called as an apostle and set apart for the gospel of God (1:1). That gospel was promised beforehand in the prophets and concerns God's Son, born of David's line and designated Son of God in power by the resurrection (1:2-4). Paul greets the believers in Rome, thanks God for their faith, longs to visit them, and says he is under obligation to Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish (1:5-15).

Observations: 'slave' (doulos) is a word of total devotion to a master; Paul lowers himself instead of trading on his fame. Unlike most of his letters, Paul names no co-sender here, though Timothy is with him (16:21): this is personal. Verses 3-4 may echo an early creed, with a parallel between 'according to the flesh' and 'according to the Spirit.' Compare 1 Timothy 3:16 and 2 Timothy 2:8, though the case is weaker than for 1 Corinthians 15:3-5.

'Designated the Son of God in power' does not mean Jesus became the Son at the resurrection; He always was. The resurrection powerfully displayed His sonship and His rule over the powers (Psalm 2; Psalm 110:1; Acts 2:32-35). Paul writes from Corinth during his three months in Greece (Acts 20:2-3), longing to visit and to be mutually encouraged.

Connections: OT servants of the LORD (Abraham, Moses, Joshua, David, the prophets, the Servant of Isaiah 40-55); Paul's call 'from my mother's womb' (Galatians 1:15) like Jeremiah's (Jeremiah 1:5); the gospel promised in Genesis 12:3, Isaiah, Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36-37; the called people of God from the nations (Hosea 2:23); the harvest (Isaiah 27:12; Matthew 9:37-38).

The lesson: before Christ, the believer's debt was to justice, and it demanded death. After Christ, the believer's debt is to grace, and it compels love and mercy, toward outsiders through the gospel and toward brothers and sisters in the church.
QUOTES: Before Christ, the Christian's debt was to justice, and it demanded death. After Christ, the Christian's debt is to grace, and it compels them to love and give mercy.
A lot of us treat the letter to the Romans as systematic theology, and that's a huge mistake. Paul is being very pastoral here with this letter.
A lot of us tend to know what we were saved from. But do we all know and appreciate what we are saved for?
Obligation to him who died produces obligation to those for whom he died.

method.h: Read a letter as a letter
method.p: Paul's letters answer real situations. Ask what was happening in the church that made him write this way. In Romans, the greeting already hints at tension between believers.

LSB_QUOTES.text: Paul, a slave of Christ Jesus, called as an apostle, having been set apart for the gospel of God,
who was designated as the Son of God in power, according to the Spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord,
I am under obligation both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to the wise and to the foolish.

left.text: Paul, a slave of Christ Jesus, called as an apostle, having been set apart for the gospel of God,

right.text: Now it happened that after these things, Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of Yahweh, died, being 110 years old.

lines.text: Doulos literally means slave. In Paul's world it meant total devotion to a master. Paul lowers himself: not 'the one and only Paul,' but a servant who belongs to Jesus.

The title has precedent. Abraham (Genesis 26:24), Moses (Joshua 1:2; 2 Kings 18:12), Joshua, David, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego (Daniel 3), the prophets (Amos 3:7) and the Servant of Isaiah 40-55 are all the LORD's servants. Low in themselves, they carry high status because God sends them.

SLAVE.title: Called and set apart
SLAVE.stamp: In the line of the prophets

left.text: But when God, who had set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through His grace, was pleased to reveal His Son in me so that I might proclaim Him as good news among the Gentiles,

right.text: “Before I formed you in the innermost parts I knew you, / And before you came out from the womb I set you apart; / I have given you as a prophet to the nations.”

lines.text: Paul is an apostle of Christ who stands in the line of the prophets: sent with God's word to Jew and Gentile alike. Like Jeremiah, he was set apart before birth for the nations.

src.text: Timothy my fellow worker greets you, and so do Lucius and Jason and Sosipater, my kinsmen.

lines.text: Paul usually names co-senders: Sosthenes (1 Corinthians), Silvanus (1 and 2 Thessalonians), Timothy (2 Corinthians, Philippians, Colossians, Philemon, 1 and 2 Thessalonians). Here he names only himself, though Timothy is with him. Whatever he says, he wants it to come from him.

PROMISE.title: Designated Son of God in power

left.text: concerning His Son, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, who was designated as the Son of God in power, according to the Spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord,

right.text: “I will surely tell of the decree of Yahweh: / He said to Me, ‘You are My Son, / Today I have begotten You. / Ask of Me, and I will surely give the nations as Your inheritance, / And the ends of the earth as Your possession.

lines.text: Did Jesus become the Son at the resurrection? No. He always was the Son, in Trinitarian relationship to the Father. The resurrection powerfully displayed His sonship and His rule over the powers that held the world.

Notice the parallel: born of David's seed 'according to the flesh,' designated Son of God 'according to the Spirit.' Some scholars hear an early creed here (compare 1 Timothy 3:16; 2 Timothy 2:8), though the case is weaker than for 1 Corinthians 15:3-5.

left.text: Yahweh says to my Lord: / “Sit at My right hand / Until I put Your enemies as a footstool for Your feet.”

right.text: This Jesus God raised up again, to which we are all witnesses. Therefore having been exalted to the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, He has poured out this which you both see and hear.

lines.text: He was already Lord when Yahweh said, 'Sit at My right hand.' Peter ties Psalm 110 to the resurrection (Acts 2:34-35); Paul says the same thing in Romans 1:4.
The resurrection was foretold too: 'many of those who sleep in the dust of the ground will awake' (Daniel 12:2); 'You will not give Your Holy One over to see corruption' (Psalm 16:10).

left.text: among whom you also are the called of Jesus Christ; to all who are beloved of God in Rome, called as saints: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

right.text: And I will sow her for Myself in the land. / I will also have compassion on her who had not obtained compassion, / And I will say to those who were not My people, / ‘You are My people!’ / And they will say, ‘You are my God!’”

lines.text: God's covenant call of His people (Isaiah 41:8-9; 43:1; 49:1) now reaches those from the nations who were not His people. Paul will lean on Hosea later in the letter (Romans 9:25-26). See also Isaiah 56:6-8.
The gospel is no new religion. Its roots are in the Scriptures: Genesis 12:3; Isaiah 11:1-10; 40:9; 52:7; 61:1; Jeremiah 31:31-34; Ezekiel 36-37.

left.text: I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that often I have planned to come to you (and have been prevented so far) so that I may have some fruit among you also, even as among the rest of the Gentiles.

right.text: Then He *said to His disciples, “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out workers into His harvest.”

lines.text: The reaping of souls is an old picture: 'you will be gathered up one by one, O sons of Israel' (Isaiah 27:12), and joy 'as with the joy of harvest' when the Child is born (Isaiah 9:3, 6). Paul draws from the prophets and from Jesus.

DEBT.title: I am a debtor
DEBT.stamp: To God and to the Gentiles

src.text: I am under obligation both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to the wise and to the foolish. In this way, for my part, I am eager to proclaim the gospel to you also who are in Rome.

lines.text: More literally, 'I am a debtor.' To whom: God or the Gentiles? Both. The gospel puts a debt on those who receive it, and the payment is to pass it on.

Why preach the gospel to Christians? They believe, yet they are missing what it means to live like Christ. Paul is setting up a pastoral correction: the grace that called him should train believers to extend mercy to each other instead of judgment.

left.text: So then, brothers, we are under obligation, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh—

right.text: For we are His workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand so that we would walk in them.

lines.text: Paul returns to the debt in Romans 8: 'you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons by whom we cry out, “Abba! Father!”' (8:15). We owe a debt to the grace that adopted us into God's family.
From condemnation to commission: love and mercy are shown in sharing the gospel with unbelievers and in how brothers and sisters treat each other as God's family.

TERMS.def: One sent with authority; Paul was 'called as an apostle' (1:1).
The good news God promised in the Scriptures, concerning His Son (1:1-3).
The obedience that comes from faith, or the obedience that is faith; the goal of Paul's apostleship among the nations (1:5; 16:26).
Most read this as the Holy Spirit, by whose power Jesus was raised (1:4; 8:11).
Greek speakers and non-Greek speakers: everyone, cultured or not (1:14).
Those set apart for God; 'called as saints' (1:7), not a special class of believers.

WORDS.gloss: Slave, bondservant; one wholly at a master's disposal. Look up: BDAG, δοῦλος.
Messenger, one sent with authority; apostle.
To determine, appoint, designate, declare. Look up: BDAG, ὁρίζω.
Slave, servant; 'servant of Yahweh' as an honored title. Look up: HALOT or BDB, עֶבֶד.

BACKGROUND.p: Most date Romans to about AD 57, written from Corinth during Paul's three months in Greece (Acts 20:2-3) before he took the collection to Jerusalem (Romans 15:25-26).

BACKGROUND.h: A church Paul had not founded
BACKGROUND.p: Believers in Rome came from Jewish and Gentile backgrounds. Paul had long wanted to visit (15:22-23) and hoped Rome would help send him on to Spain (15:24).

Acts 18:2 says Claudius ordered all Jews to leave Rome (about AD 49; compare Suetonius, Claudius 25.4). Many returned after his death in AD 54, which may help explain tensions between Jewish and Gentile believers.
Ancient letters opened with sender, recipients and greeting. Paul's opening is unusually long (1:1-7): he packs the gospel itself into the sender line.

DEBATES.p: Some ancient adoptionists read this as Jesus becoming God's Son at the resurrection. The church's historic reading, and the video's, is that the eternal Son was declared and installed 'in power' by the resurrection (compare 1:3, 'His Son,' before the resurrection is mentioned).
Many scholars see a pre-Pauline formula in the parallel lines; others think Paul wrote it freshly. The video holds it loosely.
Obedience that springs from faith, obedience that consists in faith, or both. Paul ends the letter with the same phrase (16:26).

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The video reads 'servant'; the LSB translates doulos as 'slave' (1:1), the word the video explains.
The video quotes Psalm 22:21 as 'You have rescued me from the horns of the wild oxen'; the LSB reads 'From the horns of the wild oxen You answer me.'
That Paul wrote 2 Corinthians in Macedonia (Acts 20:1) is the common view, inferred from 2 Corinthians 7:5 and 9:2-4, not stated in Acts.
Romans 1:3-4 as a creed is a scholarly proposal, as the video says; it is not certain.

QUESTIONS: Paul calls himself a slave of Christ before he calls himself an apostle. What does that order teach you?
How does the resurrection display that Jesus is the Son of God 'in power'?
Why would Paul need to preach the gospel to people who already believe it?
Paul says he is a debtor to everyone. To whom are you 'under obligation' because of grace?
Do you know what you were saved for, not only what you were saved from?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: Before Christ, our debt was to justice, and it demanded death. After Christ, our debt is to grace, and it compels us to love and to give mercy. This is a shift from condemnation to commission. Love and mercy show up in sharing the gospel with unbelievers, and also in the way brothers and sisters treat one another as God's family, which is what the Roman church was missing. Many of us know what we were saved from; Paul wants us to feel the weight of what we were saved for (Ephesians 2:10; Romans 8:12-15).
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): this week, show one concrete mercy to a believer you find hard to agree with, and pray Romans 1:8-12 for your own church.

## Summary (from the video)
- The teacher reads Romans 1:1-15. Paul introduces himself as a slave of Christ Jesus, called as an apostle and set apart for the gospel of God (1:1). That gospel was promised beforehand in the prophets and concerns God's Son, born of David's line and designated Son of God in power by the resurrection (1:2-4). Paul greets the believers in Rome, thanks God for their faith, longs to visit them, and says he is under obligation to Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish (1:5-15).
- Observations: 'slave' (doulos) is a word of total devotion to a master; Paul lowers himself instead of trading on his fame. Unlike most of his letters, Paul names no co-sender here, though Timothy is with him (16:21): this is personal. Verses 3-4 may echo an early creed, with a parallel between 'according to the flesh' and 'according to the Spirit.' Compare 1 Timothy 3:16 and 2 Timothy 2:8, though the case is weaker than for 1 Corinthians 15:3-5.
- 'Designated the Son of God in power' does not mean Jesus became the Son at the resurrection; He always was. The resurrection powerfully displayed His sonship and His rule over the powers (Psalm 2; Psalm 110:1; Acts 2:32-35). Paul writes from Corinth during his three months in Greece (Acts 20:2-3), longing to visit and to be mutually encouraged.
- Connections: OT servants of the LORD (Abraham, Moses, Joshua, David, the prophets, the Servant of Isaiah 40-55); Paul's call 'from my mother's womb' (Galatians 1:15) like Jeremiah's (Jeremiah 1:5); the gospel promised in Genesis 12:3, Isaiah, Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36-37; the called people of God from the nations (Hosea 2:23); the harvest (Isaiah 27:12; Matthew 9:37-38).
- The lesson: before Christ, the believer's debt was to justice, and it demanded death. After Christ, the believer's debt is to grace, and it compels love and mercy, toward outsiders through the gospel and toward brothers and sisters in the church.

## Key quotes from the video (auto-captions, lightly cleaned)
> "Before Christ, the Christian's debt was to justice, and it demanded death. After Christ, the Christian's debt is to grace, and it compels them to love and give mercy."
> "A lot of us treat the letter to the Romans as systematic theology, and that's a huge mistake. Paul is being very pastoral here with this letter."
> "A lot of us tend to know what we were saved from. But do we all know and appreciate what we are saved for?"
> "Obligation to him who died produces obligation to those for whom he died."

### Read a letter as a letter
Paul's letters answer real situations. Ask what was happening in the church that made him write this way. In Romans, the greeting already hints at tension between believers.

## A slave, called and set apart
1. Romans 1:1; Joshua 24:29: A slave of Christ Jesus

   (video) Doulos literally means slave. In Paul's world it meant total devotion to a master. Paul lowers himself: not 'the one and only Paul,' but a servant who belongs to Jesus.
   (video) The title has precedent. Abraham (Genesis 26:24), Moses (Joshua 1:2; 2 Kings 18:12), Joshua, David, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego (Daniel 3), the prophets (Amos 3:7) and the Servant of Isaiah 40-55 are all the LORD's servants. Low in themselves, they carry high status because God sends them. (Genesis 26:24; Joshua 1:2; 2 Kings 18:12; Amos 3:7)
2. Galatians 1:15; Jeremiah 1:5: Called and set apart
   Paul (Galatians 1:15-16, LSB): "But when God, who had set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through His grace, was pleased to reveal His Son in me so that I might proclaim Him as good news among the Gentiles,"
   Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:5, LSB): "“Before I formed you in the innermost parts I knew you, / And before you came out from the womb I set you apart; / I have given you as a prophet to the nations.”"
   (video) Paul is an apostle of Christ who stands in the line of the prophets: sent with God's word to Jew and Gentile alike. Like Jeremiah, he was set apart before birth for the nations.
3. Romans 1:1; 16:21: Paul writes alone
   A personal letter Romans 16:21: "Timothy my fellow worker greets you, and so do Lucius and Jason and Sosipater, my kinsmen." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Romans+16:21
   (video) Paul usually names co-senders: Sosthenes (1 Corinthians), Silvanus (1 and 2 Thessalonians), Timothy (2 Corinthians, Philippians, Colossians, Philemon, 1 and 2 Thessalonians). Here he names only himself, though Timothy is with him. Whatever he says, he wants it to come from him. (1 Corinthians 1:1; 2 Corinthians 1:1; Philippians 1:1)

## The gospel promised beforehand
1. Romans 1:3-4; Psalm 2:7-8: Designated Son of God in power
   Paul (Romans 1:3-4, LSB): "concerning His Son, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, who was designated as the Son of God in power, according to the Spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord,"
   David (Psalm 2:7-8, LSB): "“I will surely tell of the decree of Yahweh: / He said to Me, ‘You are My Son, / Today I have begotten You. / Ask of Me, and I will surely give the nations as Your inheritance, / And the ends of the earth as Your possession."
   (video) Did Jesus become the Son at the resurrection? No. He always was the Son, in Trinitarian relationship to the Father. The resurrection powerfully displayed His sonship and His rule over the powers that held the world.
   (video) Notice the parallel: born of David's seed 'according to the flesh,' designated Son of God 'according to the Spirit.' Some scholars hear an early creed here (compare 1 Timothy 3:16; 2 Timothy 2:8), though the case is weaker than for 1 Corinthians 15:3-5. (1 Timothy 3:16; 2 Timothy 2:8; 1 Corinthians 15:3-5)
2. Psalm 110:1; Acts 2:34-35: Sit at My right hand
   David (Psalm 110:1, LSB): "Yahweh says to my Lord: / “Sit at My right hand / Until I put Your enemies as a footstool for Your feet.”"
   Peter (Acts 2:32-33, LSB): "This Jesus God raised up again, to which we are all witnesses. Therefore having been exalted to the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, He has poured out this which you both see and hear."
   (video) He was already Lord when Yahweh said, 'Sit at My right hand.' Peter ties Psalm 110 to the resurrection (Acts 2:34-35); Paul says the same thing in Romans 1:4.
   (video) The resurrection was foretold too: 'many of those who sleep in the dust of the ground will awake' (Daniel 12:2); 'You will not give Your Holy One over to see corruption' (Psalm 16:10). (Daniel 12:2; Psalm 16:10)
3. Romans 1:6; Hosea 2:23: The called of Jesus Christ
   Paul (Romans 1:6-7, LSB): "among whom you also are the called of Jesus Christ; to all who are beloved of God in Rome, called as saints: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ."
   Hosea (Hosea 2:23, LSB): "And I will sow her for Myself in the land. / I will also have compassion on her who had not obtained compassion, / And I will say to those who were not My people, / ‘You are My people!’ / And they will say, ‘You are my God!’”"
   (video) God's covenant call of His people (Isaiah 41:8-9; 43:1; 49:1) now reaches those from the nations who were not His people. Paul will lean on Hosea later in the letter (Romans 9:25-26). See also Isaiah 56:6-8. (Isaiah 43:1; Romans 9:25-26; Isaiah 56:6-8)
   (video) The gospel is no new religion. Its roots are in the Scriptures: Genesis 12:3; Isaiah 11:1-10; 40:9; 52:7; 61:1; Jeremiah 31:31-34; Ezekiel 36-37. (Genesis 12:3; Isaiah 52:7; Jeremiah 31:31-34)

## Under obligation
1. Romans 1:13; Matthew 9:37-38: Fruit among you
   Paul (Romans 1:13, LSB): "I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that often I have planned to come to you (and have been prevented so far) so that I may have some fruit among you also, even as among the rest of the Gentiles."
   Jesus (Matthew 9:37-38, LSB): "Then He *said to His disciples, “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out workers into His harvest.”"
   (video) The reaping of souls is an old picture: 'you will be gathered up one by one, O sons of Israel' (Isaiah 27:12), and joy 'as with the joy of harvest' when the Child is born (Isaiah 9:3, 6). Paul draws from the prophets and from Jesus. (Isaiah 27:12; Isaiah 9:3)
2. Romans 1:14-15: I am a debtor
   To God and to the Gentiles Romans 1:14-15: "I am under obligation both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to the wise and to the foolish. In this way, for my part, I am eager to proclaim the gospel to you also who are in Rome." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Romans+1:14-15
   (video) More literally, 'I am a debtor.' To whom: God or the Gentiles? Both. The gospel puts a debt on those who receive it, and the payment is to pass it on.
   (video) Why preach the gospel to Christians? They believe, yet they are missing what it means to live like Christ. Paul is setting up a pastoral correction: the grace that called him should train believers to extend mercy to each other instead of judgment.
3. Romans 8:12-15; Ephesians 2:10: Saved for something
   Paul (Romans 8:12, LSB): "So then, brothers, we are under obligation, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh—"
   Paul (Ephesians 2:10, LSB): "For we are His workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand so that we would walk in them."
   (video) Paul returns to the debt in Romans 8: 'you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons by whom we cry out, “Abba! Father!”' (8:15). We owe a debt to the grace that adopted us into God's family. (Romans 8:15)
   (video) From condemnation to commission: love and mercy are shown in sharing the gospel with unbelievers and in how brothers and sisters treat each other as God's family.

## Key people
- Paul: A slave of Christ Jesus, called as an apostle, set apart for the gospel; writing from Corinth. [Background] A Pharisee trained under Gamaliel (Acts 22:3), converted on the Damascus road; he had not yet visited Rome.
- Jesus Christ our Lord: Born of David's seed; designated Son of God in power by the resurrection. [Background] The gospel is 'concerning His Son' (1:3): the letter is about Him before it is about us.
- The believers in Rome: Beloved of God, called as saints; their faith is proclaimed throughout the world. [Background] A church of Jewish and Gentile believers that Paul had not founded (15:20-22).
- Timothy: With Paul as he writes, yet not named as co-sender. [Background] Paul's 'fellow worker' (16:21), co-sender of six other letters.
- Tertius: Not mentioned. [Background] The scribe who wrote the letter down: 'I, Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord' (16:22).
- Phoebe: Not mentioned. [Background] A servant of the church at Cenchreae, Corinth's port, commended to Rome; most think she carried the letter (16:1-2).

## Places [Background]
- Corinth (named in the video): Where Paul writes, during three months in Greece (Acts 20:2-3).
- Rome (named in the video): The church Paul longs to visit (1:10-15).
- Cenchreae: Corinth's eastern port; home church of Phoebe (16:1).
- Jerusalem: Paul's next stop, with the gift for the poor (15:25-26).
- Philippi: In Macedonia, where Paul traveled before Greece (Acts 20:1-2).

## Key terms
- Apostle: One sent with authority; Paul was 'called as an apostle' (1:1).
- Gospel of God: The good news God promised in the Scriptures, concerning His Son (1:1-3).
- Obedience of faith: The obedience that comes from faith, or the obedience that is faith; the goal of Paul's apostleship among the nations (1:5; 16:26).
- Spirit of holiness: Most read this as the Holy Spirit, by whose power Jesus was raised (1:4; 8:11). [Background]
- Greeks and barbarians: Greek speakers and non-Greek speakers: everyone, cultured or not (1:14). [Background]
- Saints: Those set apart for God; 'called as saints' (1:7), not a special class of believers. [Background]

## Hebrew and Greek words [Background; Strong's numbers follow the LSB's word tagging]
- δοῦλος doulos (G1401, Greek): Slave, bondservant; one wholly at a master's disposal. Look up: BDAG, δοῦλος. (Rom 1:1)
- ἀπόστολος apostolos (G652, Greek): Messenger, one sent with authority; apostle. (Rom 1:1)
- ἀφορίζω aphorizō (G873, Greek): To separate, set apart, appoint. (Rom 1:1)
- εὐαγγέλιον euangelion (G2098, Greek): Good news, gospel. (Rom 1:1)
- ὁρίζω horizō (G3724, Greek): To determine, appoint, designate, declare. Look up: BDAG, ὁρίζω. (Rom 1:4)
- ὑπακοή hypakoē (G5218, Greek): Obedience, a hearing that submits. (Rom 1:5)
- ὀφειλέτης opheiletēs (G3781, Greek): Debtor; one under obligation. (Rom 1:14)
- עֶבֶד ʿeved (H5650, Hebrew): Slave, servant; 'servant of Yahweh' as an honored title. Look up: HALOT or BDB, עֶבֶד. (Josh 24:29)

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- When and where: Most date Romans to about AD 57, written from Corinth during Paul's three months in Greece (Acts 20:2-3) before he took the collection to Jerusalem (Romans 15:25-26).
- A church Paul had not founded: Believers in Rome came from Jewish and Gentile backgrounds. Paul had long wanted to visit (15:22-23) and hoped Rome would help send him on to Spain (15:24).
- Jews expelled, then back: Acts 18:2 says Claudius ordered all Jews to leave Rome (about AD 49; compare Suetonius, Claudius 25.4). Many returned after his death in AD 54, which may help explain tensions between Jewish and Gentile believers.
- Letter form: Ancient letters opened with sender, recipients and greeting. Paul's opening is unusually long (1:1-7): he packs the gospel itself into the sender line.

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 391): "And he calls himself, the servant of Christ, yet not merely this; for there be many sorts of servitude." Homilies on Romans 1, on 1:1. NPNF 1.11 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 391): "Casting aside the inequality of ranks, he writes to them all under one appellation." Homilies on Romans 1, on 1:7. NPNF 1.11 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 391): "I am a debtor to the Greeks and to the Barbarians, both to the wise and to the unwise. Which also he said when writing to the Corinthians. And he says it, to ascribe the whole to God." Homilies on Romans 2, on 1:14. NPNF 1.11 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- 'Designated' Son of God (1:4) Some ancient adoptionists read this as Jesus becoming God's Son at the resurrection. The church's historic reading, and the video's, is that the eternal Son was declared and installed 'in power' by the resurrection (compare 1:3, 'His Son,' before the resurrection is mentioned).
- An early creed in 1:3-4? Many scholars see a pre-Pauline formula in the parallel lines; others think Paul wrote it freshly. The video holds it loosely.
- Obedience of faith (1:5) Obedience that springs from faith, obedience that consists in faith, or both. Paul ends the letter with the same phrase (16:26).

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The video reads 'servant'; the LSB translates doulos as 'slave' (1:1), the word the video explains.
- The video quotes Psalm 22:21 as 'You have rescued me from the horns of the wild oxen'; the LSB reads 'From the horns of the wild oxen You answer me.'
- That Paul wrote 2 Corinthians in Macedonia (Acts 20:1) is the common view, inferred from 2 Corinthians 7:5 and 9:2-4, not stated in Acts.
- Romans 1:3-4 as a creed is a scholarly proposal, as the video says; it is not certain.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Paul calls himself a slave of Christ before he calls himself an apostle. What does that order teach you?
2. How does the resurrection display that Jesus is the Son of God 'in power'?
3. Why would Paul need to preach the gospel to people who already believe it?
4. Paul says he is a debtor to everyone. To whom are you 'under obligation' because of grace?
5. Do you know what you were saved for, not only what you were saved from?

## Application
- (video) Before Christ, our debt was to justice, and it demanded death. After Christ, our debt is to grace, and it compels us to love and to give mercy. This is a shift from condemnation to commission. Love and mercy show up in sharing the gospel with unbelievers, and also in the way brothers and sisters treat one another as God's family, which is what the Roman church was missing. Many of us know what we were saved from; Paul wants us to feel the weight of what we were saved for (Ephesians 2:10; Romans 8:12-15).
- Study note (added): this week, show one concrete mercy to a believer you find hard to agree with, and pray Romans 1:8-12 for your own church.
